segments.text: What are the next steps for the monitor?
Will there be more analysis of the imaging collected?
Will you go out?
Like you had said, oh, we were going to do two days and we only did one.
Are you going to go out and collect more data?
Well, for this particular project, it's at a close, but the next part of the mission is: let's get it out to the public, right?
Let's start integrating this new imagery and technology into our educational programs.
Let's get it on the website.
We do several programs working with the local schools.
Well, now let's integrate this new technology into that so now we can start inspiring that next generation of marine scientists to come out.
So that's what I look at now: our mission is we have this wonderful data which cannot live just in a filing cabinet.
It's upon us now to get it out there and make it meaningful.
And it really is incredible.
So that's that's the mission that I see next.
We're always open for new ideas at the shipwreck site, but for this particular project.
Let's get it out.
Let's make it meaningful.
Let's get it in school kids' hands.
There is a website associated with this expedition.
What are some of the most exciting things that's coming out of that website?
Yeah, well, North at Grumman have built a web portal for us.
So you can click these buttons and you can explore what we did in 2025 with the AUV in the survey and see all that incredible data, right?
And learn about it.
You know, maybe you want to be, it inspires you to be an engineer or some other part of the technical aspects of.
Of surveys.
But the other part they built on that website was they looked back at monitored in 1862, which I'm particularly excited by.
So, you know, North Agriculture has so much capability, all these different facets of things they can do.
So, one of them was building 3D models.
So, I asked them: monitors deck layout changed three times in 1862 as they learned more and did improvements.
Can you build us three different models to demonstrate that?
And they said, yeah, we can absolutely do that.

So, one of the things on the website people are going to see now are these three separate and unique monitor 3D models they can manipulate, move, and learn how monitoring changed over time, which is incredible.
We've never had that before.
And the other exciting part is, you know, when we talk about the ship sinking and what that was like, what that went through, the storm, and the incredible heroism.
Of the men that were saved by the people, the sailors of the Rhode Island that incredible night, they also created an animation of that sinking event for us.

So we can work with the conservation team here at the Marines Museum and Park, and we can look at what the artifacts told us about some of the damage and things we saw, these recovered items, like part of the monitor ske, the prop, you know, the damage that we see at the stern of the shipwreck.

How we believe the vessel sank by coming down by the stern, turning slightly to starboard, crashing into the sea floor, but crushes the stern of the vessel, which is the end of the vessel, and the right-hand side crushes that, and then everything flips upside down and lands on top.
And I believe we've recaptured that in this animation: how Noah thinks the vessel actually went down that night, December 31st, 1862.
So you've collected all of these artifacts from the monitor and brought them up.
How do you conserve them and make sure that they don't just disintegrate when they come up to the surface?
